title: 4. Broken Access Control (A01)
objective: Study-guide review — ICCS423 v2 — L10: Web Security 1 (Injection · Auth · Access Control · Sessions): 4. Broken Access Control (A01).

items: 94% of tested apps have at least one access-control flaw
Authentication ≠ authorization — knowing who doesn't say what they can do
Server-side enforcement is the only reliable layer (client checks are advisory)
Horizontal escalation — same privilege, different user (User A reads User B's order)
Vertical escalation — lower → higher privilege (regular user gains admin)
IDOR — predictable IDs in URL/body without ownership check
Path Traversal — ../../etc/passwd to escape app directory
Mass Assignment — framework binds extra fields like is_admin=true

blocks.text: ``http # Attacker logs in as user 1001, then iterates: GET /api/orders/1001 → 200 OK (own data) GET /api/orders/1002 → 200 OK (User B's data — IDOR!) GET /api/orders/1003 → 200 OK (User C's data) ``

``python # ✅ Server-side ownership check @app.route('/api/orders/<order_id>') @login_required def get_order(order_id): order = Order.query.get_or_404(order_id) if order.user_id != current_user.id: abort(403) return jsonify(order.to_dict()) ``
Real-world: Parler (2021) — sequential post IDs + no auth + no rate limit → 70TB scraped including GPS metadata of deleted posts.

items: Use UUIDs instead of sequential integers for object references
RBAC/ABAC — codify roles and attributes; enforce via decorators/middleware
Centralized authorization — one policy module (OPA, Casbin)
